Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 7 periods = 350 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 5h 50min

periods.activity_title: Broken Shell, Moving Plates: Understanding Plate Tectonics
materials: Blank outline world map (one per student or pair)
periods.visual_aids: World map showing major tectonic plates with plate boundaries marked

time_bands.activity: Open by displaying the physical world map and asking students: 'Why do the continents look like pieces of a broken puzzle?' Students suggest reasons in brief. Establish that the Earth's surface is not fixed but is made of moving tectonic plates — a large and small set of pieces forming the lithosphere (crust + upper mantle) resting on the semi-molten asthenosphere below, credited to W.J. Morgan's theory.

Walk students through the Earth's three layers — crust, mantle, core — and clarify that only the rigid lithosphere is broken into plates, while the asthenosphere's convection currents (hot material rising, cooler material sinking) drive plate movement of a few centimetres per year. Name and locate the seven major plates — Pacific, Eurasian, African, North American, South American, Indo-Australian, and Antarctic — classifying each as continental, oceanic, or mixed. Students label these on their blank outline maps using coloured pencils.

Introduce the three plate boundary types, building each with a specific real-world example: convergent (Himalaya from continental-continental collision; volcanic arcs where oceanic plate subducts beneath continental); divergent (Mid-Atlantic Ridge where rising magma builds new crust); transform (San Andreas Fault where plates slide past each other causing earthquakes). Ask: 'Which boundary type builds landforms, and which destroys them?' Students write a one-sentence answer for each boundary type on their maps.

Run the LET'S MAP activity: each student picks any two plates from their labelled map and completes a table with columns — Plate Name | Continents Carried | Oceans Carried | Boundary Type with a Named Neighbour. Then run the first LET'S EXPLORE: students overlay the plate boundary map with the earthquake-and-volcano distribution map provided and state in one sentence the pattern they see, leading to the idea of the Pacific Ring of Fire as a zone of concentrated plate-boundary activity.

periods.section_context: Major tectonic plates, convection currents, three boundary types, Ring of Fire
periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's central argument: that the Earth's surface is shaped by forces acting from within and upon it, beginning with plate tectonics as the engine of large-scale landform building. A common confusion is that students conflate the entire mantle with the asthenosphere — stress that only the upper portion is semi-molten and that it is this layer, not the whole mantle, that allows plate movement. The LET'S MAP and LET'S EXPLORE tasks anchor the theory to spatial reasoning students can verify on their own maps.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explaining important geographical concepts, the characteristics of key landforms, and their origin.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how convection currents drive plate movement and produce specific landforms at each boundary type.

competency_edges.competency_text: Locating physical phenomena on a globe or map and performing spatial-location operations.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can locate and label major tectonic plates and identify the Ring of Fire on a world map.

periods.activity_title: Earthquakes, Volcanoes, and India's Place on the Plate Map
materials: Atlas or globe (one per group of four)
Printed or projected earthquake-and-volcano distribution map
Newspaper extract on 2001 Gujarat earthquake (teacher-prepared one paragraph summary)
periods.visual_aids: Photograph of volcanic ash deposition as described in the chapter's LET'S EXPLORE box

time_bands.activity: Display the volcanic ash photograph from the chapter's LET'S EXPLORE box. Ask: 'What is the grey powder? What force produced it? What does it tell us about what is happening inside the Earth?' Students discuss in pairs for two minutes, then share. Connect their observations to the chapter's DON'T MISS OUT note on Varāhamihira's Bṛihatsaṁhitā, which recorded earthquakes — called bhūkampa — and attributed their signs to wind, rain, clouds, animal behaviour, and four elemental forces (Vāyu, Agni, Indra, Varuṇa), showing that Indians observed and theorised these phenomena long before plate tectonics.

Using the atlas, students perform the LET'S EXPLORE task: identify on the map which continents and countries lie around the Ring of Fire. Groups of four record their findings in a two-column table — Region | Why it is Earthquake/Volcano Prone — linking each region to the plate boundary type that runs through it. Draw out that the Ring of Fire traces convergent and transform boundaries around the Pacific Plate, explaining its concentration of seismic and volcanic events.

Introduce the 2001 Gujarat earthquake using the chapter's LET'S EXPLORE prompt. Students address three questions in writing: (1) Is India at risk of earthquakes? Which regions are more vulnerable and why? (2) Why do earthquakes put human lives at risk even when their magnitude is moderate? (3) What does the location of the Indo-Australian Plate's boundary tell us about India's seismic zones? Share and discuss two or three responses, correcting the common conflation of earthquake frequency with earthquake damage — damage depends on construction, population density, and preparedness.

Close with the DON'T MISS OUT note on the Baratang Island mud volcano in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands — India's only mud volcano, where underground gases and pressure push mud to the surface. Students write one sentence explaining how this phenomenon is evidence of the same internal forces discussed across the whole unit, linking it to divergent or convergent boundary activity in the region.

periods.section_context: Varāhamihira's Bṛihatsaṁhitā, bhūkampa, Gujarat earthquake, Baratang mud volcano
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the structure and movement of tectonic plates and their boundary landforms, this unit turns to the human and historical dimensions of the same forces — seismic risk, early Indian observation, and India-specific evidence of internal Earth activity. A common confusion is that students assume India is safe from earthquakes because it is not on the Ring of Fire; the Indo-Australian Plate's active convergent boundary with the Eurasian Plate (producing the Himalayas and ongoing seismicity) needs to be made explicit. The volcanic ash photograph and the Baratang mud volcano are the chapter's own observational scaffolds — use them before explaining, so students reason from evidence first.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explaining important geographical concepts, the characteristics of key landforms, and their origin.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse photographic and map evidence to infer the internal Earth processes that produce volcanic and seismic events.

competency_edges.competency_text: Critically identifying human interventions that produce or worsen environmental crises and measures to reverse them.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how human settlement patterns and construction practices increase earthquake risk and casualties.

competency_edges.competency_text: Recognising India's contributions to understanding and managing the physical environment.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can describe how early Indian scholars observed and recorded earthquake phenomena using their own conceptual frameworks.

periods.activity_title: Breaking Down and Washing Away: Weathering, Erosion, and Human Livelihoods
periods.section_anchor: Process of Weathering and Erosion / Agents of Gradation
materials: Two photographs from the chapter's LET'S EXPLORE — water erosion and wind erosion scenes
Printed or projected DON'T MISS OUT text on Sindhu-Sarasvatī water management and Zabo system
periods.visual_aids: Side-by-side photographs of water erosion gully and wind erosion desert pavement from the chapter

time_bands.activity: Display the two LET'S EXPLORE photographs — one showing water erosion and one showing wind erosion. Ask students: 'What has happened to the land in each image? What force caused it?' After brief pair discussion, introduce weathering as the in-place breakdown of rocks (no movement) and erosion as the wearing away and carrying of material by an agent. Distinguish: physical weathering (temperature change, frost, wind), chemical weathering (reactions with water, air, acids), and biological weathering (roots, organisms splitting rock).

Develop erosion across its four types — water, wind, glacial, and coastal — using the photographs as anchors for water and wind, and brief verbal description for glacial and coastal. Then shift to the LET'S EXPLORE discussion task: 'How are farmers affected by water erosion and wind erosion?' Students write three specific impacts (loss of topsoil → reduced fertility; land loss near rivers → displacement; damaged irrigation channels → crop failure) and then extend to construction, fishing, and tourism as other livelihoods named in the chapter.

Introduce the Agents of Gradation paragraph: running water, glaciers, wind, waves, and groundwater continuously lower high areas and fill low ones over time. Present the DON'T MISS OUT sidebar connecting landforms to human history — the Ganga, Nile, Brahmaputra, and Indus plains supporting agricultural societies; the Himalayas as both barrier and corridor (Khyber Pass); the Thar Desert's Silk Route; and coasts as centres of trade. Ask: 'Why did early civilisations settle on river plains rather than in mountains or deserts?' Students write a two-sentence geographical explanation.

Present the DON'T MISS OUT passage on Sindhu-Sarasvatī water management: contouring, bunding, terracing, dams, and canals documented in the Vedas, Kṛiṣhiparāśhara, Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra, and Vṛikṣhāyurveda. Add the Zabo system of Nagaland — earthen bunds and check dams on hillslopes conserving soil and water and recharging groundwater. Students write one sentence each: (a) Why were these techniques necessary given the erosion processes just studied? (b) What principle of human-environment relationship do they represent?

periods.section_context: Three weathering types, four erosion types, Sindhu-Sarasvatī techniques, Zabo system
periods.teacher_notes: Having established the internal forces that build landforms, this unit introduces the external forces that wear them down, grounding the processes in their effects on real human occupations and in India's documented traditions of environmental management. A common confusion is that students treat weathering and erosion as synonyms — the decisive distinction is movement of material, which only erosion involves. The Sindhu-Sarasvatī and Zabo passages are the chapter's own primary evidence of an Indian conservation ethos; students should be pushed to connect these practices causally to the erosion processes they have just analysed, rather than treating them as separate cultural facts.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explaining important geographical concepts, the characteristics of key landforms, and their origin.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can distinguish weathering from erosion by type and mechanism and explain how gradation agents shape the surface over time.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analysing the inter-relationship between human beings and their physical environment, including nature-conservation practices.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how erosion processes affect specific human livelihoods and explain why river plains became centres of early civilisation.

competency_edges.competency_text: Developing sensitivity to the conservation of soil and water resources and the measures taken to protect them.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can connect traditional Indian soil-and-water conservation techniques to the erosion processes they were designed to counter.

competency_edges.competency_text: Recognising India's contributions to understanding and managing the physical environment.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can cite specific texts and traditions as evidence of India's systematic approach to managing erosion and conserving water.

periods.activity_title: Rivers at Work: Valleys, Waterfalls, Meanders, and Deltas
materials: Cross-section diagram of a river's upper, middle, and lower course (teacher-drawn or printed)
Blank three-column table for students (Upper Course | Middle Course | Lower Course)
periods.visual_aids: Annotated river-course diagram showing V-valley and waterfall (upper), meander and oxbow lake (middle), delta and levee (lower)

time_bands.activity: Display the river-course diagram and establish the organising idea: a river performs erosion, transportation, and deposition in different proportions at different stages of its journey, and each stage produces characteristic landforms. Upper course: fast-moving water on steep gradients cuts downward, forming V-shaped valleys, rapids, and waterfalls — where hard rock resists erosion but soft rock below wears away, the river drops over a cliff edge. Ask: 'What human uses does a waterfall offer?' — hydroelectric power, tourism, recreation, cultural or religious significance. Students record the landforms and uses in the upper-course column of their table.

Middle course: gradient lessens, lateral erosion dominates over vertical. Demonstrate how the outer bank of a curve erodes while the inner bank receives deposition, gradually widening bends into meanders and eventually cutting off loops into oxbow lakes. Fertile floodplain soil builds up along the meander belt, supporting agriculture and dense settlement. Introduce the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) in Tamil Nadu as a historical example of using a meandering river for irrigation — a human adaptation to the depositional processes of the middle course. Students fill the middle-course column.

Lower course: gradient nearly flat, sediment load is deposited where river meets sea, ocean, or lake, building a fan-shaped or triangular delta of rich alluvial soil. Deltas are ideal for rice and jute cultivation, important fishing grounds where fresh and saltwater mix, and centres of dense settlement and trade, though prone to flooding. Run the LET'S EXPLORE task on the Sundarbans delta: students write three reasons why the Sundarbans is unique (largest mangrove delta, UNESCO site, biodiversity including Bengal tiger) and one reason it attracts tourists — connecting delta formation to ecological and economic significance.

Students complete their three-column table with a fourth row: 'Human significance of landforms in this course section.' Then each student writes one sentence for each course stage explaining the cause-and-effect chain: gradient → erosion/deposition balance → landform → human use. Select two or three to share; correct any conflation of transportation and deposition.

periods.section_context: V-valleys, waterfalls, meanders, Kallanai, oxbow lakes, Sundarbans delta
periods.teacher_notes: The unit builds on the distinction between erosion and deposition established earlier, now applying it spatially along a river's course to show how gradient governs which landforms emerge. A common confusion is that students think all rivers form deltas — many rivers do not reach still water or carry insufficient sediment, so the delta is a specific set of conditions, not a universal outcome. The Kallanai and Sundarbans examples are the chapter's own anchors for human significance and should be used to demonstrate, not merely mentioned.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explaining important geographical concepts, the characteristics of key landforms, and their origin.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a cause-and-effect account of how river gradient governs the landforms produced at each stage of a river's course.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analysing the inter-relationship between human beings and their physical environment, including nature-conservation practices.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how river-formed landforms at different course stages shape agricultural, settlement, and trade opportunities for human communities.

periods.activity_title: Waves, Ice, and Wind: Coastal, Glacial, and Arid Landforms
materials: Printed or projected images of a sea cliff and stack, a U-shaped glacial valley, and a barchan dune
THINK ABOUT IT prompt on the 2021 Chamoli flood (teacher-printed from the chapter)
periods.visual_aids: Three-panel image: coastal erosion sequence (cave → arch → stack), glacial U-valley with moraine, and barchan dune field

time_bands.activity: Display the coastal erosion panel and ask: 'How does a sea cliff become a stack?' Walk students through the sequence: waves undercut a headland to form a cave, the cave breaks through to an arch, the arch roof collapses leaving an isolated stack. Distinguish deposition landforms (beach — sand, pebbles, rock deposited along the shoreline, valuable for tourism, fishing, and as a natural wave barrier) from erosion landforms (cliffs, wave-cut platforms, arches, stacks) along the same coast. Students sketch the formation sequence with a one-line label for each stage.

Move to the glacial valley panel. Glaciers — slow-moving bodies of ice — erode rock by plucking and abrasion, carving U-shaped valleys (as distinct from river-carved V-shapes), cirques, aretes, hanging valleys, and fjords. Introduce moraines — till (rock, soil, debris) deposited as a glacier melts — classifying lateral (sides), terminal (front), and medial (where two glaciers meet) moraines, and noting their fertile soil and role as natural dams forming lakes used for irrigation and hydropower. Present the THINK ABOUT IT prompt on the February 2021 Chamoli flood: students write a causal chain of at least three steps explaining how glacial lake outburst, moraine dam failure, or ice detachment could have triggered the flood and its downstream destruction.

Shift to the arid panel. Wind lifts loose sand and soil to create yardangs (streamlined rock ridges), ventifacts (sandblasted polished rocks), deflation hollows or blowouts (shallow depressions), and desert pavements (flat surfaces after fine particles are removed). Then wind deposits material in dunes: barchan (crescent-shaped), longitudinal (parallel ridges), star, and parabolic — each shaped by wind direction and sand supply. Students add a row to the panel sketch naming each wind landform and identifying whether it is erosional or depositional.

Brief whole-class synthesis comparison: 'What is the key difference between the valley a glacier carves and the valley a river carves, and what does each valley offer to people who live near it?' Students write one sentence. Then: 'Which of the three agents — waves, glaciers, or wind — has the most significant human uses in its depositional landforms, and why?' Students write a one-sentence justified claim, drawing on tourism, agriculture, freshwater, and coastal protection uses named across the three sections.

periods.section_context: Cave-arch-stack sequence, U-valleys, moraines, Chamoli flood, barchan and other dunes
periods.teacher_notes: This unit covers three distinct erosional agents in a single sitting, so the organising frame — each agent's characteristic erosion sequence leading to specific landforms with specific human uses — must be made explicit at the outset and revisited at the close. A common confusion is that students treat the U-shape vs. V-shape distinction as arbitrary; stress that the width of glacial erosion (plucking broad walls of rock) vs. the downward cutting of a river is the causal explanation, not simply a shape label. The Chamoli prompt is the chapter's own inquiry scaffold and should be the analysis vehicle for the glacial section, not a supplementary item.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explaining important geographical concepts, the characteristics of key landforms, and their origin.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare the formation sequences, characteristic landforms, and cross-agent distinctions produced by waves, glaciers, and wind.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analysing the inter-relationship between human beings and their physical environment, including nature-conservation practices.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the human significance of depositional and erosional landforms created by waves, glaciers, and wind for livelihoods and resource use.

competency_edges.competency_text: Critically identifying human interventions that produce or worsen environmental crises and measures to reverse them.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a causal chain linking glacial processes and human vulnerability to explain a sudden glacial flood disaster.

periods.activity_title: Water Beneath the Rock: Karst Landforms and Underground Water
materials: Diagram of karst topography showing cave interior with stalactites and stalagmites, sinkholes, and underground rivers
Printed LET'S EXPLORE prompt on local landform observation
periods.visual_aids: Karst topography cross-section diagram: surface sinkholes (dolines), underground cave passage, stalactites hanging from ceiling, stalagmites rising from floor, underground river

time_bands.activity: Display the karst cross-section diagram. Ask: 'What is dissolving the rock to create these features, and why does it only happen here?' Establish the mechanism: groundwater in limestone or other soluble rock becomes slightly acidic (absorbing carbon dioxide), slowly dissolving the rock through chemical weathering over long periods. This creates Karst topography — a landscape shaped not by surface agents but by water moving through rock. Name and locate each feature on the diagram: caves (underground chambers), stalactites (hanging from ceiling), stalagmites (rising from floor), sinkholes or dolines (surface depressions where rock has collapsed), and underground rivers.

Explore the human significance of karst landforms: caves provide fresh groundwater and are sites of tourism, adventure, and geological study; stalactites and stalagmites attract geologists and adventurers; caves carry cultural or religious significance in many societies. Ask: 'Why might a sinkhole be a problem for a town built above a karst landscape?' Students write a causal explanation. Then ask: 'How is karst cave formation different from the caves formed by wave action on a headland?' Students write a one-sentence comparison naming the agent and the rock type involved in each.

Run the LET'S EXPLORE activity: students observe landforms around their school or home (or recall features from their home region) and identify which agent of gradation may have created them — running water, waves, glaciers, wind, or groundwater. Each student writes three observations in the format: Landform observed | Likely agent | How I can tell. Share three or four examples across the class, using each to consolidate the characteristic signatures of each agent.

Close with a comparison table students build in their notebooks with columns: Agent | Landform type (erosional/depositional) | Key landform example | Primary rock or material acted on | One human use. Students populate rows for running water, waves, glaciers, wind, and groundwater from their accumulated knowledge. This is a within-unit consolidation of the full Agents of Gradation arc, completed here rather than carried forward.

periods.section_context: Karst topography, stalactites, stalagmites, sinkholes, underground rivers in limestone
periods.teacher_notes: Having covered surface agents driven by kinetic energy (running water, waves, glaciers, wind), this unit introduces groundwater as an agent that works through chemical rather than mechanical energy — an important conceptual contrast. A common confusion is that students conflate stalactites and stalagmites, or think both hang from the ceiling; the mnemonic that stalac-tites hold tight to the ceiling while stalag-mites grow from the ground is reliable. The closing comparison table is a within-unit consolidation activity, not a cross-unit product — it draws only on what students have encountered in their own unit experience.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explaining important geographical concepts, the characteristics of key landforms, and their origin.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how chemical weathering by groundwater produces karst landforms and contrast this mechanism with mechanical surface erosion.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analysing the inter-relationship between human beings and their physical environment, including nature-conservation practices.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify how karst landforms provide and constrain human water supply, settlement, and economic activity.

periods.activity_title: When Landforms Become Hazards: Landslides, Avalanches, GLOFs, and Dust Storms
materials: Newspapers (two or three issues, any recent date) or printed news summaries of a recent Indian landslide, avalanche, or GLOF event

time_bands.activity: Open with the LET'S EXPLORE prompt from the chapter: students scan the newspapers or printed summaries to identify two disaster-prone areas in India or the world and note what type of disaster occurred and one mitigation measure mentioned. Share findings briefly. Establish the unit's organising question: 'How do the same landforms that support human life also generate natural disasters, and what role do human actions play?'

Work through landslides and avalanches in parallel, building each as a combination of natural and human factors. Landslides: heavy continuous rainfall (adds weight, reduces friction), earthquakes shaking slopes, steep terrain with loose or weathered rock, and human activities — deforestation, mining, road and hillside construction, poor drainage and land use. Avalanches: heavy snowfall over weak layers, temperature rise reducing friction, wind piling snow unevenly, and triggers from skiing, trekking, construction, and earthquakes. Ask: 'In both cases, which human activities increase risk, and what does that tell us about how we use mountain environments?'

Introduce GLOFs (Glacial Lake Outburst Floods): rapid glacier melting raises lake levels, heavy rain or snow adds water, and earthquakes, avalanches, or landslides collapse the ice or moraine dam, releasing destructive floods downstream — damaging settlements, roads, bridges, and hydroelectric projects. Connect to the 2021 Chamoli event. Then cover dust storms: strong winds lift loose dry soil and sand, aggravated by drought and low rainfall, sparse vegetation from deforestation, overgrazing, poor farming, and climate change. Ask students to identify which of these causal factors are natural and which are human-accelerated.

Students complete the LET'S EXPLORE task in writing: construct a two-column table — Disaster Type | Human Activities That Worsen It | One Mitigation Measure — for all four disasters. Then each student writes a final paragraph: 'The same forces that build the landforms supporting human agriculture, settlement, and trade can also destroy human lives. What principle of human-environment relationship does this reveal, and what does it demand of us?' Share two or three responses. Close by connecting the chapter's full argument: internal forces build; external forces reshape; both create hazards that require understanding and preparation.

periods.section_context: Landslides, avalanches, GLOFs, dust storms — natural and human causal factors
periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the full arc of the chapter's content — plate tectonics, weathering, erosion, and gradation agents — now framed through the lens of disaster causation and the human role in amplifying risk. A common confusion is that students treat natural disasters as purely natural, missing the chapter's explicit argument that deforestation, mining, overgrazing, and construction are named causal factors across all four disaster types. The closing reflective paragraph is designed to complete its full cycle within this unit — the prompt, the writing, and the sharing all occur here, so no continuation is needed or implied.

competency_edges.competency_text: Critically identifying human interventions that produce or worsen environmental crises and measures to reverse them.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can critically analyse the human activities that intensify landslide, avalanche, GLOF, and dust storm disasters and propose evidence-based mitigation measures.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analysing the inter-relationship between human beings and their physical environment, including nature-conservation practices.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a reasoned argument about the reciprocal relationship between landform use and natural disaster risk.

competency_edges.competency_text: Developing sensitivity to the conservation of soil and water resources and the measures taken to protect them.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify specific conservation and mitigation measures that reduce disaster risk in landform-sensitive environments.

los.implied_lo: Students can cite specific texts and traditions as evidence of India's systematic approach to managing erosion and conserving water.

competency.competency_text: Explaining important geographical concepts, the characteristics of key landforms, and their origin.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse photographic and map evidence to infer the internal Earth processes that produce volcanic and seismic events.
assessment_items.question_text: A photograph shows a thick layer of fine grey powder covering rooftops, fields, and trees across a wide area near a coastline. Which combination of evidence would most strongly support the conclusion that a volcanic eruption near a convergent plate boundary caused this deposit — and NOT an eruption at a divergent boundary?

options.label: A
options.text: The deposit is located near an ocean trench, and seismic records show a deep-focus earthquake immediately before the eruption.

options.label: B
options.text: The deposit is located near a mid-ocean ridge, and the rock beneath it is made of fresh basalt.

options.label: C
options.text: The grey powder is rich in calcium carbonate, which indicates it originated in a limestone cave system below the surface.

options.label: D
options.text: The area receives heavy rainfall, which could have washed ash from a distant location regardless of the boundary type.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Allow students to annotate the option they select with a brief reason (one phrase), making reasoning visible without requiring extended writing.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses divergent boundary features (mid-ocean ridges, basalt) with convergent boundary volcanism — student has not distinguished boundary types by their products.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses volcanic ash with limestone cave material — student is mixing the chemical weathering agent (groundwater dissolving limestone) with internal earth processes, showing a category error.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Avoids plate tectonic reasoning altogether and substitutes a surface process (rainfall transport), indicating the student has not applied the boundary-type framework to evidence interpretation.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a cause-and-effect account of how river gradient governs the landforms produced at each stage of a river's course.
assessment_items.question_text: A river begins in high mountains and ends at the sea. Explain how a change in gradient from the upper course to the lower course changes the balance between erosion and deposition, and name one landform produced at each stage as evidence of that change.
expected_elements: States that steep gradient in the upper course gives water high energy, causing dominant vertical (downward) erosion.
Names a landform from the upper course produced by this vertical erosion — V-shaped valley, waterfall, or rapids.
States that gradient flattens in the lower course, reducing water energy and shifting dominance to deposition.
Names a landform from the lower course produced by deposition — delta, levee, or alluvial fan.
Connects gradient change causally to the erosion-deposition balance shift (not merely listing landforms).
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who struggle with extended writing may use a labelled diagram with a two-column annotation (upper course | lower course) to show the same causal reasoning.

competency.competency_text: Explaining important geographical concepts, the characteristics of key landforms, and their origin.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare the formation sequences, characteristic landforms, and cross-agent distinctions produced by waves, glaciers, and wind.
assessment_items.question_text: Read the source provided and answer the questions that follow.

sub_questions.label: a
sub_questions.text: According to the source, what process creates a sea arch, and from what earlier landform does it develop?

sub_questions.label: b
sub_questions.text: The source says arches 'eventually collapse.' Using your knowledge of wave action on headlands, explain the sequence of landforms from headland to stack.

sub_questions.label: c
sub_questions.text: A glaciated valley and a wave-eroded headland are both reshaped by erosion. Using the source and your knowledge, compare the agent, mechanism, and characteristic shape produced in each case, and explain why the resulting landforms look so different.

visual_stimulus.payload:
Where waves attack a headland from both sides, they may carve sea caves into the base of the cliff. If two caves on opposite sides of a headland meet, they form a sea arch — a bridge of rock with open water beneath it. Arches are temporary landforms; the roof is weakened by continued wave erosion and eventually collapses, leaving an isolated pillar of rock called a stack standing in the sea. Stacks are slowly worn down to low rocky platforms at the waterline. The same waves that erode these features deposit sand, pebbles, and shell fragments along quieter stretches of the coast, building beaches that act as natural barriers absorbing wave energy.
— Chapter summary account of coastal wave action

assessment_items.inclusivity: For students with reading difficulties, the teacher may read the passage aloud once before students respond. Sub-question (a) may be answered in point form.

SOURCE_INTERPRETATION.stimulus_rationale: The coastal erosion sequence — cave to arch to stack — is explicitly named in the chapter's Waves and Currents section as a key erosional landform sequence. This source passage presents that sequence in the chapter's own language, making it a direct stimulus for the section's content. It is naturally suited to an ascending-demand set: reading the sequence (Understanding), applying it to reconstruct the full headland-to-stack process (Analysis), and comparing it with glacial erosion across agent, mechanism, and shape (Analysis).
sub_question_expectations: Sub-question (a): Student identifies wave erosion attacking opposite sides of a headland, forming caves that meet to create a sea arch; the arch develops from caves.

Sub-question (b): Student correctly sequences — headland → cave (wave undercutting base) → arch (caves meet through headland) → stack (arch roof collapses) → wave-cut platform (stack eroded to waterline) — with a causal link at each step.

Sub-question (c): Strong response names agent (waves vs. glacier), mechanism (wave hydraulic action and abrasion vs. glacial plucking and abrasion), and characteristic shape (cliffs/stacks — irregular, vertical faces vs. U-shaped valley — smooth, broad, rounded floor and walls), explaining that water acts laterally at a fixed shoreline while ice moves through and excavates a valley floor and walls over its whole path.

competency.competency_text: Explaining important geographical concepts, the characteristics of key landforms, and their origin.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how chemical weathering by groundwater produces karst landforms and contrast this mechanism with mechanical surface erosion.
assessment_items.question_text: A geologist examining a limestone landscape finds sinkholes on the surface, underground rivers in cave passages below, and stalactites and stalagmites inside those caves. Explain how each of these three features forms through groundwater action, and contrast the mechanism that creates them with the mechanism by which a river carves a V-shaped valley. In your answer, name the type of weathering involved in each case.
look_for: Explains the mechanism accurately: groundwater absorbs CO₂ to become mildly acidic and dissolves limestone through chemical weathering over long periods.
Accounts for sinkholes/dolines as surface collapses where rock below has been dissolved, leaving an unsupported roof.

Accounts for stalactites as mineral-rich water dripping from the cave ceiling and depositing calcium carbonate as it evaporates, and stalagmites as deposits building upward from drips falling to the cave floor.
Names the agent of karst formation as chemical weathering (or chemical erosion by groundwater), contrasting it with physical/mechanical erosion by river water cutting downward through rock.
Identifies V-shaped valley formation as mechanical erosion — river water's kinetic energy abrading and cutting the rock, carrying material downstream.
Draws a clear conceptual contrast: karst works by dissolving the mineral structure of rock (chemistry); river valleys work by physically removing rock particles (mechanics/kinetic energy).
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use a two-column table (Karst / River valley) to organise their response before writing prose, or submit the table alone if prose writing is challenging.

competency.competency_text: Explaining important geographical concepts, the characteristics of key landforms, and their origin.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how convection currents drive plate movement and produce specific landforms at each boundary type.
assessment_items.task: You are preparing an information card for a geology museum display titled 'How Moving Plates Shape the Earth.' Create a cause-effect map that traces the journey from convection currents in the mantle to a specific landform at each of the three plate boundary types. Your map must show the causal chain (not just list steps) and include a named real-world example for each boundary type.
assessment_items.scaffold: Step 1 — Start with the energy source: What drives the convection currents? (heat from the core) → Step 2 — What do convection currents do to the plates above them? → Step 3 — At a CONVERGENT boundary: what happens when plates meet? → Name a landform produced and a real-world example. → Step 4 — At a DIVERGENT boundary: what happens when plates pull apart? → Name a landform produced and a real-world example. → Step 5 — At a TRANSFORM boundary: what happens when plates slide past each other? → Name a hazard or feature and a real-world example. → Step 6 — Add arrows on your map to show the direction of cause and effect at each stage.
format_of_output: A cause-effect map with labelled boxes or nodes connected by directional arrows
At least one named real-world example at each of the three boundary types
A brief title for the completed map
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use words alone (a flowchart in text) rather than a drawn diagram if spatial layout is difficult. Bilingual labels are acceptable on the map.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: This task reveals whether students have internalised the causal logic of plate tectonics — not just boundary names and landform labels, but the energy source → plate movement → boundary interaction → landform outcome chain — and can apply it to produce an explanatory structure using real-world anchors.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold breaks the causal chain into six checkpoints to prevent students from stopping at a list of boundary types. Check that students have included the heat-from-core → convection → plate movement chain before they reach boundary types, and that arrows show direction of causation rather than mere sequence.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: Arrows or connectors show cause-effect direction at every step; each boundary type includes a named example (e.g., Himalaya for convergent, Mid-Atlantic Ridge for divergent, San Andreas Fault for transform); the energy source (mantle heat) appears as the chain's starting node. Weak: Steps are listed as a numbered sequence without causal connectors; boundary types are labelled but examples are generic ('mountains', 'earthquakes') without a named location; the map starts from plate boundaries rather than from the convection energy source.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A cause-effect map is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO because the LO requires students to show how one process (convection) drives another (plate movement) which produces specific outcomes (landforms at each boundary type). A linear cause-effect structure makes the causal chain explicit and examinable, and the chapter's own LET'S EXPLORE activities on plate-boundary correlation prime students for this connective thinking. The teacher may substitute any other format from the Open Task menu — a comparison table of boundary types, a structured discussion with written output, or a source analysis task on the LET'S EXPLORE volcanic ash evidence — as each can equally demonstrate this LO.

competency.competency_text: Analysing the inter-relationship between human beings and their physical environment, including nature-conservation practices.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse how erosion processes affect specific human livelihoods and explain why river plains became centres of early civilisation.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Process of Weathering and Erosion / Agents of Gradation
assessment_items.question_text: A farmer near a river finds that his topsoil has been stripped by water erosion over several years, reducing crop yields. A construction engineer nearby reports that riverbank land is increasingly unstable for new buildings. A fisherman notes that fine sediment in the river has reduced fish populations. Which statement best analyses the common underlying geographical process linking all three observations?

options.label: A
options.text: Biological weathering by plant roots is loosening the soil, making it vulnerable to all three problems simultaneously.

options.label: B
options.text: Water erosion is transporting surface material away from the river area, stripping fertility, destabilising banks, and depositing sediment that disrupts aquatic ecosystems.

options.label: C
options.text: Chemical weathering is changing the mineral composition of the soil and river water, producing all three effects through alteration of material rather than removal.

options.label: D
options.text: Deposition of material brought from upstream is building up the riverbed, which raises water levels and is the common cause of all three livelihood problems.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses biological weathering (in-place breakdown by organisms) with erosion, and does not recognise that weathering alone does not transport or deposit material — student has not applied the weathering-vs.-erosion distinction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Substitutes chemical weathering (mineral alteration) for water erosion (physical removal and transport) — student understands that a process is acting on material but misidentifies which process connects removal, destabilisation, and sedimentation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Substitutes deposition as the agent, reversing the erosion direction — student has recalled that rivers transport and deposit material but has not applied the concept that these three effects are consequences of material being removed from the site rather than added to it.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how river-formed landforms at different course stages shape agricultural, settlement, and trade opportunities for human communities.
assessment_items.question_text: A geographer argues: 'The physical characteristics of a river's lower course make it the most important stretch of a river for human civilisations.' Using specific landforms from the lower course, evaluate whether this claim is justified.
expected_elements: Identifies at least two lower-course landforms — delta, levee, alluvial fan, or floodplain — and names their physical characteristics (e.g., flat terrain, rich alluvial soil, proximity to sea or lake).
Links each named landform to a specific human use — agriculture (rice, jute), dense settlement, fishing (freshwater-saltwater mixing), or trade and transport.

Either supports or qualifies the geographer's claim with a stated reason — e.g., lower-course fertility and delta trade nodes justify the claim, OR an upper-course waterfall's hydropower or a meander belt's irrigation also matter.
Uses geographical reasoning to justify the evaluation, not just assertion.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may respond using a brief table (Landform | Physical characteristic | Human use) followed by one evaluative sentence rather than continuous prose.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a reasoned argument about the reciprocal relationship between landform use and natural disaster risk.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter argues that the same landforms that support human life — mountains, river plains, glacial valleys, and desert regions — also generate the disasters that destroy it. Using two contrasting landform types from the chapter, construct a reasoned argument that evaluates this claim. Your argument should address both what the landform offers and how it endangers, and it should explain what this reciprocal relationship demands of people who live in or use these environments.
look_for: Selects two genuinely contrasting landform types (e.g., mountain slope vs. river delta; glacial valley vs. desert plain) rather than two that present similar relationships.

For each landform, states at least one concrete human benefit (agriculture, freshwater, trade, tourism, settlement) and at least one specific disaster linked to that landform (landslide, GLOF, flood, dust storm).
Identifies at least one human activity that intensifies the disaster risk — deforestation, mining, poor construction, overgrazing — for at least one of the two landforms.
Constructs a stated evaluative position on whether the claim is justified, rather than only describing each landform.

Draws a conclusion about what the reciprocal relationship demands — preparedness, sustainable use, conservation measures, or land-use regulation — grounded in the chapter's content rather than generic advice.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to construct a written argument may use a structured frame: 'Landform A offers __ but endangers __ because __. Landform B offers __ but endangers __ because __. This shows that people who live here must __.'' This frame captures the full reasoning in simpler sentence structures.

competency.competency_text: Critically identifying human interventions that produce or worsen environmental crises and measures to reverse them.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can critically analyse the human activities that intensify landslide, avalanche, GLOF, and dust storm disasters and propose evidence-based mitigation measures.
assessment_items.question_text: A hillside in a mountain region has been deforested for road construction over several years. A period of heavy continuous rainfall then triggers a large landslide. A government report recommends replanting trees, banning further road cutting, and improving drainage channels as mitigation measures. Which statement best evaluates the connection between the human interventions, the disaster, and the proposed mitigation?

options.label: A
options.text: Deforestation and road construction are irrelevant to the landslide, because heavy continuous rainfall is a purely natural trigger that operates independently of land use.

options.label: B
options.text: Deforestation removed root systems that held soil, and road cutting created unstable slopes, together reducing friction and adding weight that heavy rainfall then exploited — the mitigation measures directly address each human-caused factor.

options.label: C
options.text: The landslide was caused solely by the weight of rainfall water on the slope, so replanting trees is the only relevant mitigation, and road construction had no additional effect.

options.label: D
options.text: Road construction actually stabilises slopes by compacting the soil, so it reduces landslide risk, and the report's recommendation to ban road cutting is therefore incorrect.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Treats natural triggers and human interventions as independent rather than interacting — student has not grasped that human land-use choices alter the physical conditions that determine how a natural trigger plays out.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Partially accepts the human-environment link (accepts deforestation) but dismisses road construction as a causal factor — student applies the chapter's framework selectively rather than to all named human interventions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Inverts the causal relationship for road construction, applying a misconception that compaction equals stability on slopes, ignoring that road cutting removes material from the slope face and creates instability.

competency.competency_text: Critically identifying human interventions that produce or worsen environmental crises and measures to reverse them.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how human settlement patterns and construction practices increase earthquake risk and casualties.
assessment_items.question_text: Two towns lie in the same seismic zone with identical earthquake frequency. Town A has strict building codes requiring earthquake-resistant construction; Town B has no such codes and many old, unreinforced brick buildings. When an earthquake of equal magnitude strikes both towns, Town B suffers far more casualties. Evaluate: is this difference in casualties evidence of a failure of geography or a failure of governance?
expected_elements: Recognises that both towns face the same physical hazard — same seismic zone, same earthquake frequency and magnitude — so the difference in casualties is not explained by geography alone.
Identifies that human decisions (building codes, construction standards, land-use planning) determine how physical hazard translates into human disaster.
Takes a stated position: the higher casualties in Town B are primarily evidence of a governance failure (absence of construction regulation) rather than a geographical difference.

Supports the position with at least one specific mechanism from the chapter — e.g., unreinforced brick buildings collapse under seismic shaking; earthquake-resistant design absorbs and distributes seismic energy.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may state their position in one sentence and support it with two brief bullet points rather than a paragraph, if prose structuring is a barrier.

competency.competency_text: Locating physical phenomena on a globe or map and performing spatial-location operations.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can locate and label major tectonic plates and identify the Ring of Fire on a world map.
assessment_items.question_text: A student is labelling a world map and needs to correctly identify the Pacific Ring of Fire. Which description accurately locates it and explains why the plate boundaries there produce both earthquakes and volcanoes?

options.label: A
options.text: The Ring of Fire runs along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge because divergent boundaries there constantly produce magma that erupts as both volcanoes and earthquakes.

options.label: B
options.text: The Ring of Fire encircles the Pacific Ocean along convergent and transform boundaries where subducting oceanic plates generate volcanic arcs and earthquake zones.

options.label: C
options.text: The Ring of Fire is located at the centre of the Pacific Ocean along the transform boundaries of the Pacific Plate, where plates slide horizontally past each other.

options.label: D
options.text: The Ring of Fire runs through the Eurasian Plate interior, where ancient fold mountains such as the Himalayas produce concentrated volcanic activity.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the Ring of Fire with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, placing it on a divergent boundary — student has memorised 'Ring of Fire = volcanic' but not its location around the Pacific or its convergent-boundary origin.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Places the Ring of Fire in the Pacific interior rather than around its perimeter, and assigns only transform boundaries — student partially recalls transform faults (San Andreas) but has not grasped that the Ring traces the Pacific Plate's edges, dominated by subduction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Displaces the Ring of Fire to the Eurasian Plate interior and confuses fold mountain formation (convergent collision between continental plates) with the subduction-driven volcanic arc activity that defines the Ring of Fire.

competency.competency_text: Developing sensitivity to the conservation of soil and water resources and the measures taken to protect them.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect traditional Indian soil-and-water conservation techniques to the erosion processes they were designed to counter.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Process of Weathering and Erosion / Agents of Gradation
assessment_items.question_text: The Zabo system of Nagaland uses earthen bunds and check dams placed on hillslopes to manage water. Which statement best explains how this system addresses the specific erosion risk of a hillslope environment?

options.label: A
options.text: Earthen bunds on hillslopes prevent chemical weathering by stopping rainwater from reacting with the mineral surface of rocks.

options.label: B
options.text: Earthen bunds and check dams slow the downslope flow of water, reducing its erosive energy, trapping sediment, and allowing water to seep into the ground rather than run off.

options.label: C
options.text: The Zabo system works by adding mineral nutrients to the soil through the decomposition of the earthen material used to build the bunds.

options.label: D
options.text: Check dams channel water rapidly off the slope into the valley below, preventing waterlogging of the hillside soil and protecting it from erosion by weight.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses water erosion (physical removal of material by moving water) with chemical weathering (mineral alteration by reactions) — student has recalled both processes but misidentified which one the Zabo system targets.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misidentifies the mechanism as nutrient addition rather than water-flow control — student has recognised that the system improves land condition but has substituted a biological/chemical explanation for the hydrological one.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Inverts the water-management logic: the Zabo system slows and retains water on the slope; this option describes rapid removal, which would increase erosive energy and sediment loss rather than reduce them.

competency.competency_text: Developing sensitivity to the conservation of soil and water resources and the measures taken to protect them.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify specific conservation and mitigation measures that reduce disaster risk in landform-sensitive environments.
assessment_items.question_text: A district in a hilly region is prone to landslides. Local officials are considering four measures: (i) planting trees on denuded slopes, (ii) opening new quarries for road construction stone, (iii) building drainage channels to divert rainwater away from slopes, and (iv) relocating settlements away from the steepest slopes. Identify which two measures are most effective at reducing landslide risk, and explain for each how it addresses a specific causal factor named in the chapter.
expected_elements: Selects measures (i) and (iii), or (i) and (iv), as the two most effective — both address named causal factors (vegetation loss increases instability; poor drainage adds water weight and reduces friction; settlement on steep slopes increases exposure).
Explains for measure (i) that tree roots anchor soil and reduce water runoff on slopes, countering the deforestation factor the chapter names as a landslide cause.

Explains for measure (iii) that drainage channels reduce the weight of water on the slope and maintain friction by keeping soil drier, countering heavy rainfall's contribution to landslide risk, OR explains for measure (iv) that relocating settlements reduces human exposure on slopes identified as unstable.
Identifies measure (ii) — quarrying — as counterproductive, OR does not select it, demonstrating that mining is a named human activity the chapter associates with increased landslide risk.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may number their chosen measures and explain each in one sentence rather than a paragraph.

competency.competency_text: Recognising India's contributions to understanding and managing the physical environment.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how early Indian scholars observed and recorded earthquake phenomena using their own conceptual frameworks.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter notes that Varāhamihira's Bṛihatsaṁhitā described signs and causes of earthquakes, which early Indians called 'bhūkampa.' What does this text most accurately demonstrate about early Indian engagement with physical phenomena?

options.label: A
options.text: Varāhamihira correctly identified convection currents in the mantle as the cause of earthquakes, anticipating the theory of plate tectonics by centuries.

options.label: B
options.text: Early Indian scholars systematically observed environmental signs associated with earthquakes and developed conceptual frameworks to explain them, even though their causal models differed from modern plate tectonics.

options.label: C
options.text: The Bṛihatsaṁhitā shows that Indians only used religious or mythological explanations for earthquakes and made no empirical observations of the natural world.

options.label: D
options.text: Because Varāhamihira attributed earthquakes to four elemental forces, his text has no scientific value and represents pre-rational thinking about natural events.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Overclaims by projecting modern plate tectonics back onto Varāhamihira — student recognises the text's relevance but has not distinguished between systematic observation/conceptual explanation and the specific modern theory.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Underclaims by treating the elemental-force framework as purely mythological, missing the chapter's explicit record of observed environmental signs (wind, rain, clouds, animal behaviour) which are empirical observations within a different conceptual framework.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Dismisses the text's value on grounds that its causal model differs from modern science — student has not grasped that systematic observation and concept formation have intellectual value independent of whether the causal model matches a later paradigm.

competency.competency_text: Recognising India's contributions to understanding and managing the physical environment.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can cite specific texts and traditions as evidence of India's systematic approach to managing erosion and conserving water.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Process of Weathering and Erosion / Agents of Gradation
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter mentions that water management practices of the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation are documented in the Vedas, Kṛiṣhiparāśhara, Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra, and Vṛikṣhāyurveda. Name two specific techniques described in these texts, and explain what each technique was designed to achieve in relation to soil or water management.
expected_elements: Names two techniques from the chapter's list: contouring, bunding, terracing, dams, or canals (the Zabo system is also acceptable as a named tradition).

For each technique, states what it was designed to achieve — e.g., terracing creates flat planting surfaces on slopes to slow water runoff and prevent soil erosion; bunding creates barriers to trap water and sediment; canals distribute water across farmland.
Demonstrates that the student understands these as purposeful soil-or-water management interventions, not merely engineering structures.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use a two-row table (Technique | What it achieves) rather than prose.
